bridges.mechanism: A reduction in the physical flow of crude, diesel or LNG tightens near-term supply relative to demand and pushes up cash (spot) prices for oil and refined fuels.

A drop in Russian hydrocarbon exports forces EU buyers to outcompete Asian buyers for alternative LNG/oil cargoes and charter capacity, raising freight and energy input costs and causing a measurable contraction in China‑EU manufactured goods trade volumes as supply chains and shipping slots are reallocated.

A net reduction in physical hydrocarbon deliveries to global markets tightens available supply relative to demand and, through direct supply–demand mechanics, raises spot prices (and conversely increased flow depresses spot prices).
Reductions in Russia-related hydrocarbon flows (pipeline outages, export curbs) tighten immediate physical availability in global markets, driving benchmark crude and diesel prices up within weeks.

Declines in overland or proximate seaborne Russian supply force rerouting of tankers onto chokepoints and longer routes, concentrating traffic and raising opportunities for Iran-linked proxies to harass, seize or attack vessels and terminals.

A rise in successful or attempted attacks on production, refining, storage or transport nodes directly increases the assessed probability that key maritime, pipeline or transit corridors will be disrupted or denied due to damage, closures or heightened military/escort requirements.

Increased kinetic attacks on pipelines, terminals and coastal energy facilities create operational precedents and opportunistic targeting patterns that raise the perceived and actual risk of hostile actions against tankers servicing routes between Asia and Europe, prompting insurers and operators to treat tanker transits as higher‑risk.

Increased frequency of successful attacks on production, pipelines, terminals or export facilities directly removes physical export capacity and interrupts shipping routes, immediately lowering aggregate crude movement through the system.

A rise in successful attacks on production, refining or export nodes elevates insurance and transport risk premia and can degrade local processing capacity, which raises delivered oil and diesel prices even beyond direct supply metrics.

Increased short- to medium-term variability in wholesale energy prices propagates into broader commodity and derivatives markets, raising measured financial market volatility as hedgers and speculators adjust positions and margining.

Elevated collective uncertainty about future supply, demand and policy prompts authorities to escalate regulatory, fiscal or emergency interventions (e.g., releases, price controls, advisories) to stabilize markets and reassure participants.

Sharp increases in market uncertainty lead producers, traders and carriers to pull back on forward commitments and run down inventories, producing tangible interruptions in delivery schedules and localized shortages that disrupt the steady flow of energy deliveries between suppliers and EU/Asian buyers.

Rising uncertainty about future supply/demand encourages commercial and strategic actors to build precautionary onshore and floating stocks, increasing aggregate storage volumes as insurance against shocks.

Elevated uncertainty about future supply and policy prompts traders and governments to expand precautionary stocks and charter/hold floating storage, increasing measured global crude and product inventories over the coming months.

Aggressive energy‑market interventions (sanctions, price caps, export controls and subsidies) by the EU and its partners in response to the war increase regulatory frictions and compliance costs for cross‑border transactions, slowing customs/contract flows and reducing bilateral China‑EU trade volumes as firms restructure supply chains.

Stronger policy actions (sanctions, export bans, rerouting mandates or designated-port restrictions) force cargoes onto longer or constrained routes and displace eligible tonnage, increasing demand for available tankers and pushing up charter rates.
Higher global crude and product stocks provide a buffer against supply shocks from regional proxy disruptions, thereby reducing short-term price swings and derivative-market volatility.
Larger global crude and refined fuel stocks act as a buffer against supply interruptions arising from the Iran proxy theater, reducing the magnitude and frequency of short‑term oil price swings.
Higher accumulated on‑hand crude and product stocks increase readily available supply to the market, directly lowering spot market price pressure.

An uptick in proxy attacks on tankers, ports or pipelines directly raises the assessed probability of disruption along maritime and pipeline corridors as insurers, shippers and navies adjust risk ratings and routings.

Frequent hostile incidents attributed to Iran-linked proxies increase retaliatory strikes, diplomatic escalations and force-readiness among regional states, raising aggregate geopolitical conflict intensity.

An increased rate of hostile incidents against energy/logistics actors normalizes and expands operational targeting patterns, directly raising the probability and expected frequency of attacks on commercial tankers and port operations.
A rise in attacks/seizures on tankers, terminals or pipelines forces shutdowns, port closures and diversion of cargoes, directly lowering the physical rate of crude movement.
More frequent security incidents increase insurance premiums, require rerouting and demand for safer/longer voyages, raising spot tanker charter costs and risk surcharges.

More frequent Iran-proxy attacks on tankers, pipelines and terminals cause physical disruptions and route diversions (longer voyages, tightened insurance, port closures) that immediately reduce net delivered hydrocarbon volumes to global markets.

A rise in episodic security incidents in Middle Eastern shipping lanes produces sudden shipment uncertainty and stop‑start flows, provoking larger intraday and near‑term swings in oil and diesel prices.
Higher oil and diesel prices raise transport and manufacturing costs for energy‑intensive goods, prompting firms to cut or delay cross‑border shipments and thereby lowering China–EU trade flows.

Iran-related upward pressure on energy prices forces governments to enact visible policy measures (strategic reserve releases, emergency subsidies, sanction waivers or procurement shifts) that change the intensity and timing of policy actions tied to the Russia–Ukraine energy/political response set.

Broader sanctions and export controls prompt trading partners and affected states to enact emergency policy responses (tariffs, stock releases, export bans or subsidies) to stabilize supplies and political fallout.

Stricter sanctions and export controls tied to Iran-proxy escalation directly block counterparties, increase compliance and insurance costs, and curtail routes or counterpart access, reducing China–EU trade volumes on affected goods.

Expanded sanctions and trade controls legally prohibit or complicate exports from affected producers and traders, directly reducing the volume of crude legitimately moving through global trade channels.

Expansion or tightening of trade/sanctions against Iran or its proxies increases ambiguity about future access to certain shipping routes, counterparties and insurance, raising market participants' uncertainty about near‑term supply and policy trajectories relevant to the Russia–Ukraine energy context.

Sharp rises in oil spot prices prompt rapid government interventions (SPR releases, subsidies, export controls, taxes or advisories) aimed at stabilizing markets or shielding consumers, increasing policy action intensity.

Sharp, sustained increases in oil spot prices lead governments to implement temporary export controls, price caps or licensing restrictions (to shield domestic markets or punish adversaries), thereby raising trade and sanction measures.

Sharp rises in spot oil prices drive inflation and fiscal stress, prompting governments and central banks to deploy subsidies, price controls, strategic releases, or monetary/fiscal interventions aimed at stabilizing markets.

An increase in aggregate crude flows raises near-term supply available to markets and physical delivery, directly reducing immediate scarcity and pushing spot prices down (and vice versa when flows drop).

Higher aggregate crude flow directly raises the quantity of energy cargoes moving through international routes, increasing measured trade flow volumes between producers and major consumers (including China and the EU).
Increased crude tanker traffic raises the density of valuable, soft targets and transit interactions in chokepoints, modestly raising the probability of hostile incidents against shipping.

A sustained drop in global crude flow (especially through MENA choke points) increases Tehran's incentive to use proxy attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure to raise costs, signal deterrence and extract political leverage, driving up the frequency of security incidents.

An increase in the aggregate crude flow rate eases tightness in physical markets and reduces the sensitivity of prices to discrete disruptions, thereby damping short- to medium-term wholesale price swings.

Higher onshore and nearshore hydrocarbon stocks reduce the need for emergency policy measures because authorities view inventories as a buffer and are less likely to trigger releases or extraordinary controls.
Larger onshore and nearshore hydrocarbon inventories provide a buffer that can be drawn down to cover production or transit outages, directly lowering the observed rate of supply disruptions.

Rapid draws in global storage inventories prompt consuming and transit states to impose export restrictions, rationing or priority allocation rules to preserve domestic supplies, increasing the overall level of trade restrictions.

Higher onshore and nearshore hydrocarbon stocks reduce ambiguity about near-term supply availability and buffer against shocks, thereby lowering collective market uncertainty among traders and policymakers.

Spikes in tanker charter rates raise uncertainty about delivery timing and costs, increasing basis risk and hedging activity which amplifies price swings and financial market volatility in the short term.

Rising tanker charter rates increase shipping costs and freight-rate uncertainty, prompting firms to cut or reroute shipments and reducing bilateral trade volumes between high-volume partners such as China and the EU.

Sustained increases in tanker charter rates raise transport costs and reduce the economic viability of some shipments, causing charter cancellations, longer voyage times or route avoidance that lower net physical deliveries to destination markets.

Escalating interstate conflict raises war premiums, reduces available safe/insured tonnage (via flagging and owner withdrawals), and lengthens voyages through detours, driving up charter costs for tankers.

A rise in geopolitical conflict intensity prompts states and coalitions to impose new sanctions, export controls and transit restrictions aimed at adversaries or their partners, expanding the scope and severity of trade restrictions relevant to Iran and its proxies.

An increase in overall geopolitical conflict intensity raises incentives, resources and operational cover for kinetic strikes, sabotage and proxy attacks against production, refining and transport nodes, increasing the frequency of energy-infrastructure attacks.
Rising assessed risk along key sea lanes prompts opportunistic state and non‑state actors to target lightly escorted tankers and raises the measured probability of attacks.
Higher route security risk forces shippers to reroute, slow transit, and pay much higher insurance/premiums, directly reducing the volume of energy cargoes moved between regions.

Rising security risks (attacks, mines, seizures or interdictions) cause port closures, convoying, rerouting around longer corridors and temporary shut-ins, directly reducing the physical throughput of crude shipments.
Elevated route risks generate an immediate supply-risk premium and anticipatory buying (and insurance surcharges), pushing up spot prices even before large physical flow reductions materialize.

An increased assessed risk to key routes reflects more hostile activity and weaker escorts, which directly raises opportunities and incentives for Iran-aligned proxy groups and other malign actors to attack or seize tankers, pipelines and convoys, increasing incident frequency.

Higher assessed risk to key maritime, pipeline or air corridors leads to rerouting, port shutdowns, convoy slowdowns and insurance refusals that directly reduce the net physical flow of crude, refined fuels and LNG into markets.

Higher spot commodity prices raise the potential payoff from capturing or disrupting energy shipments, which increases incentives for Iran-aligned proxies and opportunistic actors to mount attacks on energy logistics, raising incident frequency.

Sharp increases in spot oil and gas prices trigger governments and regulators to deploy fiscal and regulatory measures (strategic reserve releases, subsidies, price controls, export rules) to blunt economic impacts, elevating the intensity of policy responses.
Elevated financial-market volatility increases speculative positioning and rapid risk re‑pricing in oil futures, directly amplifying short‑term crude price swings.

Elevated financial-market volatility forces margining, rapid position adjustments and shifting risk premia among traders and funds, which amplifies short- to medium-term wholesale energy price swings.

New export controls, sanctions or emergency trade measures implemented by governments (e.g., export bans, licensing requirements) immediately reduce cross‑border energy and dual‑use flows between China and EU counterparties.
Intense policy actions in a crisis frequently include coordinated strategic reserve releases or mandated emergency sales that directly reduce on‑hand hydrocarbon inventories.

An increase in interventionist policies (sanctions, export bans, port denials) directly curtails cross-border flows and commercial shipments, causing regional stored volumes to be stranded and lowering accessible global crude and fuel inventories.
An increase in geopolitical incidents and coercive measures linked to China–EU rivalry injects a risk premium into markets and prompts short‑term supply concerns, lifting global oil spot prices.

An acute escalation in China–EU geopolitical friction draws diplomatic attention, political capital and budgetary/military resources away from Ukraine-related programs, causing EU/NATO actors to scale back or delay fiscal and military policy measures aimed at the Russia–Ukraine war.
Actual interruptions to energy production, refining or transport reduce immediate available cargoes in spot markets, forcing buyers to bid up cash prices for oil and refined fuels.

Escalation of China–EU trade measures (sanctions, export controls or port denials) directly interrupts production, export approvals and transit of crude and refined shipments between facilities, reducing the aggregate physical crude movement rate.
Interruptions to production, refining or transport caused by China–EU trade friction directly reduce available near-term supply and push benchmark crude and refined-product prices higher.
Larger and more frequent crude-price swings transmit through futures, options and correlated instruments, amplifying volatility across commodity and related financial markets.

Rising short‑term oil price volatility driven by China–EU trade shocks incentivizes traders and some governments to increase onshore and near‑shore stockpiles as a hedge, raising aggregate storage volumes.

Spikes in oil-price volatility driven by China–EU trade shocks propagate through global futures and physical-arbitrage channels into Brent/Urals-linked trading, directly increasing wholesale price variability in energy markets connected to the Russia–Ukraine conflict.

A rise in the perceived probability and expected frequency of tanker attacks directly elevates the assessed likelihood of disruption along maritime chokepoints and shipping lanes, increasing overall route security risk as operators reroute, delay sailings, or require escorts.
Higher perceived risk of hostile actions against tankers tied to China–EU rivalry raises insurance and security costs and shrinks available safe-flag capacity, driving up the cost to charter vessels.

Escalation of China–EU naval shadowing, interdiction attempts or sanction-driven convoying raises both opportunities and incentives for Iran-aligned proxy groups to mount more attacks on tankers and ports to exploit confused maritime security conditions.

Sustained reductions in China–EU trade volumes increase political and economic pressure to deploy regulatory and fiscal interventions (tariffs, export controls, subsidies, stock releases), so higher trade flows tend to reduce the need for such policy interventions.
Reduced China–EU cross-border shipments of crude and refined products lead to fewer tanker/loadings into storage hubs, directly drawing down world commercial fuel stocks.

nodes.label: Capital flow volatility

nodes.label: Policy response level
nodes.description: Magnitude and intensity of monetary, fiscal and regulatory actions directed at energy markets and macroeconomic stabilization.

nodes.label: Inflationary pressure
nodes.description: Broad upward pressure on consumer and producer prices attributable in part to changes in energy costs and supply disruptions.

nodes.label: Energy-transition investment rate
nodes.description: Flow of capital deployed into low-carbon energy technologies, infrastructure and related transition activities per unit time.

nodes.label: Strategic reserve level
nodes.description: Quantity held in strategic petroleum or fuel reserves available for deliberate release to stabilize markets.

nodes.label: Aggregate central bank monetary stance

nodes.label: Trade and sanctions restriction level

nodes.label: Diesel flow rate

nodes.description: The average transit time for tanker voyages between major loading and unloading hubs, capturing rerouting and delays across the system.

nodes.label: Aviation route availability

nodes.label: Travel safety advisory intensity
nodes.description: The aggregated frequency and severity of official travel and safety advisories affecting air and surface transport operations across jurisdictions.

nodes.label: Geopolitical conflict intensity
nodes.description: The overall level of armed conflict and interstate or regional military confrontation exerting pressure on energy and transport systems, measured continuously.

nodes.label: Non-state attack rate

nodes.label: Commodity derivatives open interest

nodes.label: Currency volatility

nodes.label: Energy demand rate

Sharp, sustained increases in oil spot prices lead governments to implement temporary export controls, price caps or licensing restrictions (to shield domestic markets or punish adversaries), thereby raising trade and sanction measures.

Sharp rises in spot oil prices drive inflation and fiscal stress, prompting governments and central banks to deploy subsidies, price controls, strategic releases, or monetary/fiscal interventions aimed at stabilizing markets.

An increase in aggregate crude flows raises near-term supply available to markets and physical delivery, directly reducing immediate scarcity and pushing spot prices down (and vice versa when flows drop).

Higher aggregate crude flow directly raises the quantity of energy cargoes moving through international routes, increasing measured trade flow volumes between producers and major consumers (including China and the EU).
Increased crude tanker traffic raises the density of valuable, soft targets and transit interactions in chokepoints, modestly raising the probability of hostile incidents against shipping.

A sustained drop in global crude flow (especially through MENA choke points) increases Tehran's incentive to use proxy attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure to raise costs, signal deterrence and extract political leverage, driving up the frequency of security incidents.

An increase in the aggregate crude flow rate eases tightness in physical markets and reduces the sensitivity of prices to discrete disruptions, thereby damping short- to medium-term wholesale price swings.

Higher onshore and nearshore hydrocarbon stocks reduce the need for emergency policy measures because authorities view inventories as a buffer and are less likely to trigger releases or extraordinary controls.
Larger onshore and nearshore hydrocarbon inventories provide a buffer that can be drawn down to cover production or transit outages, directly lowering the observed rate of supply disruptions.

Rapid draws in global storage inventories prompt consuming and transit states to impose export restrictions, rationing or priority allocation rules to preserve domestic supplies, increasing the overall level of trade restrictions.

Higher onshore and nearshore hydrocarbon stocks reduce ambiguity about near-term supply availability and buffer against shocks, thereby lowering collective market uncertainty among traders and policymakers.

Spikes in tanker charter rates raise uncertainty about delivery timing and costs, increasing basis risk and hedging activity which amplifies price swings and financial market volatility in the short term.

Rising tanker charter rates increase shipping costs and freight-rate uncertainty, prompting firms to cut or reroute shipments and reducing bilateral trade volumes between high-volume partners such as China and the EU.

Sustained increases in tanker charter rates raise transport costs and reduce the economic viability of some shipments, causing charter cancellations, longer voyage times or route avoidance that lower net physical deliveries to destination markets.

Escalating interstate conflict raises war premiums, reduces available safe/insured tonnage (via flagging and owner withdrawals), and lengthens voyages through detours, driving up charter costs for tankers.

A rise in geopolitical conflict intensity prompts states and coalitions to impose new sanctions, export controls and transit restrictions aimed at adversaries or their partners, expanding the scope and severity of trade restrictions relevant to Iran and its proxies.

An increase in overall geopolitical conflict intensity raises incentives, resources and operational cover for kinetic strikes, sabotage and proxy attacks against production, refining and transport nodes, increasing the frequency of energy-infrastructure attacks.
Rising assessed risk along key sea lanes prompts opportunistic state and non‑state actors to target lightly escorted tankers and raises the measured probability of attacks.
Higher route security risk forces shippers to reroute, slow transit, and pay much higher insurance/premiums, directly reducing the volume of energy cargoes moved between regions.

Rising security risks (attacks, mines, seizures or interdictions) cause port closures, convoying, rerouting around longer corridors and temporary shut-ins, directly reducing the physical throughput of crude shipments.
Elevated route risks generate an immediate supply-risk premium and anticipatory buying (and insurance surcharges), pushing up spot prices even before large physical flow reductions materialize.

An increased assessed risk to key routes reflects more hostile activity and weaker escorts, which directly raises opportunities and incentives for Iran-aligned proxy groups and other malign actors to attack or seize tankers, pipelines and convoys, increasing incident frequency.

Higher assessed risk to key maritime, pipeline or air corridors leads to rerouting, port shutdowns, convoy slowdowns and insurance refusals that directly reduce the net physical flow of crude, refined fuels and LNG into markets.

Higher spot commodity prices raise the potential payoff from capturing or disrupting energy shipments, which increases incentives for Iran-aligned proxies and opportunistic actors to mount attacks on energy logistics, raising incident frequency.

Sharp increases in spot oil and gas prices trigger governments and regulators to deploy fiscal and regulatory measures (strategic reserve releases, subsidies, price controls, export rules) to blunt economic impacts, elevating the intensity of policy responses.
Elevated financial-market volatility increases speculative positioning and rapid risk re‑pricing in oil futures, directly amplifying short‑term crude price swings.

Elevated financial-market volatility forces margining, rapid position adjustments and shifting risk premia among traders and funds, which amplifies short- to medium-term wholesale energy price swings.

New export controls, sanctions or emergency trade measures implemented by governments (e.g., export bans, licensing requirements) immediately reduce cross‑border energy and dual‑use flows between China and EU counterparties.
Intense policy actions in a crisis frequently include coordinated strategic reserve releases or mandated emergency sales that directly reduce on‑hand hydrocarbon inventories.

An increase in interventionist policies (sanctions, export bans, port denials) directly curtails cross-border flows and commercial shipments, causing regional stored volumes to be stranded and lowering accessible global crude and fuel inventories.
An increase in geopolitical incidents and coercive measures linked to China–EU rivalry injects a risk premium into markets and prompts short‑term supply concerns, lifting global oil spot prices.

An acute escalation in China–EU geopolitical friction draws diplomatic attention, political capital and budgetary/military resources away from Ukraine-related programs, causing EU/NATO actors to scale back or delay fiscal and military policy measures aimed at the Russia–Ukraine war.
Actual interruptions to energy production, refining or transport reduce immediate available cargoes in spot markets, forcing buyers to bid up cash prices for oil and refined fuels.

Escalation of China–EU trade measures (sanctions, export controls or port denials) directly interrupts production, export approvals and transit of crude and refined shipments between facilities, reducing the aggregate physical crude movement rate.
Interruptions to production, refining or transport caused by China–EU trade friction directly reduce available near-term supply and push benchmark crude and refined-product prices higher.
Larger and more frequent crude-price swings transmit through futures, options and correlated instruments, amplifying volatility across commodity and related financial markets.

Rising short‑term oil price volatility driven by China–EU trade shocks incentivizes traders and some governments to increase onshore and near‑shore stockpiles as a hedge, raising aggregate storage volumes.

Spikes in oil-price volatility driven by China–EU trade shocks propagate through global futures and physical-arbitrage channels into Brent/Urals-linked trading, directly increasing wholesale price variability in energy markets connected to the Russia–Ukraine conflict.

A rise in the perceived probability and expected frequency of tanker attacks directly elevates the assessed likelihood of disruption along maritime chokepoints and shipping lanes, increasing overall route security risk as operators reroute, delay sailings, or require escorts.
Higher perceived risk of hostile actions against tankers tied to China–EU rivalry raises insurance and security costs and shrinks available safe-flag capacity, driving up the cost to charter vessels.

Escalation of China–EU naval shadowing, interdiction attempts or sanction-driven convoying raises both opportunities and incentives for Iran-aligned proxy groups to mount more attacks on tankers and ports to exploit confused maritime security conditions.

Sustained reductions in China–EU trade volumes increase political and economic pressure to deploy regulatory and fiscal interventions (tariffs, export controls, subsidies, stock releases), so higher trade flows tend to reduce the need for such policy interventions.
Reduced China–EU cross-border shipments of crude and refined products lead to fewer tanker/loadings into storage hubs, directly drawing down world commercial fuel stocks.
